title_en: 财保北京支公司 v. 铜河公司 & 寰宇公司 — dispute over subrogation claim under a contract of carriage of goods by sea
ruling_gist_en: 1. When performing its delivery obligation under a contract of carriage of goods by sea, the carrier shall deliver the goods in accordance with the description of the goods on the clean bill of lading. Even if the carrier proves, by the outturn report at the loading port, that the goods actually received or loaded on board are inconsistent with the description on the clean bill of lading, the consignee still has the right, in accordance with Article 77 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, to take delivery of the goods from the carrier according to the contents recorded on the bill of lading.

full_text_en:
PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Beijing Direct Branch v. Copper River Maritime Inc. and Pan Cosmos Shipping & Enterprises Co., Ltd. — subrogation dispute arising from a contract of carriage of goods by sea

Ruling Summary

1. When performing the delivery obligation under a contract of carriage of goods by sea, the carrier shall deliver the goods in accordance with the description of the goods on the clean bill of lading. Even if the carrier presents the loading port ullage report to prove that the quantity of goods actually received or loaded on board differs from that recorded on the clean bill of lading, the consignee still has the right, pursuant to Article 77 of the Maritime Code, to take delivery of the goods from the carrier based on the contents recorded on the bill of lading.

2. Where the crude oil trade contract and the transport documents do not stipulate the method of measurement for cargo delivery at the loading and discharging ports, and various different measurement methods are actually used during the delivery, such as flow meter measurement, shore tank measurement, and vessel ullage measurement, and under such circumstances, the consignee claims a shortage of goods based on the discrepancy between the quantity recorded in the shore tank measurement certificate at the discharging port and that recorded in the bill of lading, but the shore tank measurement data provided by the consignee occurred outside the carrier's period of responsibility, and the consignee cannot provide other valid evidence to prove that the crude oil shortage occurred during the carrier's period of responsibility, while the carrier defends itself by presenting the ullage reports and dry tank reports at the loading and discharging ports which are consistent with the bill of lading, the actual quantity of crude oil delivered may be determined based on the ullage reports and dry tank reports. The weight certificate of the measurement shore tank provided by the consignee shall not be effective in proving the quantity of crude oil delivered, unless the carrier has consented thereto.

Plaintiff: PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Beijing Direct Branch; domiciled at Chengming Building, No. 2, South Xizhimen Street, Xicheng District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Yang Bin, Deputy General Manager of the Branch.

Defendant: Copper River Maritime Inc.; domiciled at Bankboston Building, Espanay Calle Elvira Mendez Street, Panama City, Republic of Panama.

Legal Representative: Liao Weiwen, Director of the Company.

Defendant: Pan Cosmos Shipping & Enterprises Co., Ltd.; domiciled at Room 3601-3602, 36/F, West Tower, Shun Tak Centre, 168-200 Connaught Road Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Liao Weiwen, Director of the Company.

The plaintiff, PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Beijing Direct Branch (hereinafter referred to as PICC Beijing Branch), filed an action with the Ningbo Maritime Court of the People's Republic of China against the defendants, Copper River Maritime Inc. (hereinafter referred to as Copper River) and Pan Cosmos Shipping & Enterprises Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Pan Cosmos), in a subrogation dispute arising from a contract of carriage of goods by sea.

The plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch, alleged that: On May 7, 2002, the plaintiff insured 28,835 tons of Cinta crude oil imported by China International United Petroleum & Chemicals Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as China International Petrochemical Company), which was shipped from Cinta, Indonesia to Zhoushan, China. The master of the vessel "Xique," which carried the cargo, issued a clean bill of lading No. CINTA-2607 on behalf of the shipowner. The vessel "Xique" arrived at the port of destination, Zhoushan, on May 15, 2002, and completed discharge on May 17, 2002. The Zhejiang Entry-Exit Inspection and Quarantine Bureau, Inspection and Quarantine Technical Center (hereinafter referred to as CCIQ) inspected the cargo and issued Weight Certificate No. 70200YJ25, certifying that the actual discharge quantity of the "Xique" was 28,339.606 tons, a shortage of 495.394 tons compared with the bill of lading quantity. The plaintiff, in accordance with the insurance contract, paid insurance compensation to the insured for the relevant losses suffered, totaling USD 67,497.62, and lawfully obtained the right of subrogation. The vessel "Xique" is owned by the defendant Copper River and actually operated and managed by the defendant Pan Cosmos. The defendants carried the cargo and issued a clean bill of lading, but failed to deliver the cargo as described in the bill of lading in full and in good condition, and shall bear corresponding liability for compensation. The plaintiff requested the court to order the defendants to pay USD 67,497.62 for the cargo loss and USD 674.98 in interest. During the trial, as the insured's actual payment for the goods was reduced due to a price reduction, the plaintiff amended the claims, reducing the compensation amount claimed from the defendants to USD 65,802.40.

The plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch, submitted the following evidence:

1. Commercial invoice dated May 13, 2002 and its copy, payment voucher for the cargo, and trade contract, to prove the price of the cargo in question;
2. Clean bill of lading No. CINTA-2607, to prove the contents of the contract of carriage of goods and the quantity of the cargo;
3. Certificate of cargo quantity at the loading port, to prove that the carrier determined the weight of the cargo based on shore-side data at the loading port and issued the clean bill of lading;
4. CCIQ Weight Certificate and its appendix, and inspection confirmation form for the condition of the discharge pipeline, to prove that the discharge quantity of the "Xique" at the port of destination was 28,339.606 tons;
5. Insurance policy, receipt and letter of subrogation, insurance indemnity remittance voucher, and receipt confirmation list issued by the insured, China International Petrochemical Company, to prove that the plaintiff has paid insurance indemnity to the insured under the cargo insurance contract and lawfully obtained the right of subrogation;
6. Letter of guarantee issued by the P&I Club, to prove that the owner of the vessel "Xique" is the defendant Copper River and that the vessel was not under a bareboat charter;
7. CCIQ's ship/shore quantity comparison table and empirical coefficient table for other vessels, to prove that the empirical coefficient of the vessel is 1.00312, indicating that the vessel's measurement data is on the high side and should be corrected, and also that the oil temperature during discharge was low, which might cause oil to adhere to the tank walls and result in incomplete discharge.

The defendants, Copper River and Pan Cosmos, submitted the following defense: Copper River, as the registered owner of the vessel "Xique," had transported the cargo to the port of destination in good condition on May 15, 2002, in accordance with the contract of carriage of goods by sea, and had fully discharged the cargo by May 17, 2002, thereby fulfilling all contractual obligations. The plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch, has no right to demand the carrier to deliver the cargo at the port of destination according to the cargo weight (28,835 tons) recorded in the bill of lading. A bill of lading is only prima facie evidence of the quantity of goods received by the carrier at the loading port, not absolute evidence. The trade contract for the cargo provided by the plaintiff stipulated that the ullage report at the loading port should be one of the documents for the seller to receive payment. The loading port ullage report was signed by the loading port terminal manager, the chief officer of the "Xique," and the surveyor, and therefore is binding on both the consignee and the carrier. In fact, the plaintiff knew or should have known the discrepancy between the cargo weight recorded in the bill of lading and that recorded in the loading port ullage report, and raised no objection when paying and taking delivery of the bill of lading and the loading port ullage report. This conduct in fact indicates that the plaintiff acknowledged and accepted the weight difference, and thus has lost the right to demand the carrier to deliver the cargo at the port of destination based on the cargo weight recorded in the bill of lading. The plaintiff's claim is based on the CCIQ Weight Certificate, but the data in this certificate were calculated based on the liquid depth measured before and after the crude oil in question was discharged from the carrier vessel into the C-05 shore tank at Aoshan Oil Depot. Any cargo discrepancy reflected therein, even if it exists, occurred outside the carrier's period of responsibility, and the defendants should not bear any liability for it. According to the ullage report of the "Xique" at the port of destination, the total quantity of cargo on board before discharge was 28,693.417 tons, which was also confirmed by the signature of the CCIQ surveyor on the report, and is close to the total cargo quantity of 28,835 tons recorded in the bill of lading, with the discrepancy falling within the tolerance allowed by international practice in the maritime oil transportation industry. Furthermore, according to the dry tank report issued by the vessel, there was no residual oil in any of the cargo tanks containing the cargo in question, and this dry tank report was confirmed by the signature of the consignee's representative. In conclusion, there is no shortage of cargo whatsoever, and the plaintiff's claims should be dismissed.

The defendants, Copper River and Pan Cosmos, submitted the following evidence:

1. Ullage report and dry tank report of the vessel "Xique" at the port of destination before discharge, to prove that before discharge, upon the signature of the CCIQ surveyor and the consignee's representative, it was confirmed that there was no residual crude oil in the cargo tanks of the "Xique" containing the cargo in question, and that the quantity discharged from the vessel was 28,693.417 tons, with no shortage;
2. Cargo tank calibration table of the "Xique" certified by the China Classification Society, to prove the basis for calculating the cargo capacity recorded in the ullage report;
3. Statement of Ouyang Chunhui, the chief officer of the "Xique," to prove the relevant facts during the loading, voyage, and discharge of the voyage in question;
4. Ullage report at the loading port, to prove that the actual loaded quantity of crude oil on the "Xique" was 28,680.549 tons.

The Ningbo Maritime Court ascertained the following facts:

On April 25, 2002, China International Petrochemical Company entered into a sales contract with Unipec Asia Company Ltd. for the import of 28,835 tons of Cinta crude oil, stipulating: the quantity of crude oil was 210,000 barrels (with a tolerance of ±5%), the price was USD 26.239 per barrel CIF Zhoushan; payment by T/T 30 days after signing of documents; the accompanying documents were invoice, bill of lading, certificate of quantity, ullage report, etc. The contract did not stipulate the method of measurement for cargo delivery at the loading and discharging ports. On May 6 of the same year, the cargo was insured by the plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch. The insurance policy stipulated: the insured was China International Petrochemical Company, the insured cargo was 28,835 tons of Cinta crude oil, and the insured amount was USD 5,541,676.80. From May 6 to 7 of the same year, the cargo was loaded on the vessel "Xique" at Cinta Port, Indonesia, into cargo tanks No. 1 (port, center, starboard), No. 3, Slop tanks (port and starboard), and No. 5 center tank. On May 7 of the same year, the master of the "Xique" issued a clean bill of lading No. CINTA-2607 based on the certificate of quantity measured by flow meter issued by the shipper and the survey company at the loading port. The bill of lading stated a net weight at 60°F of 211,200 barrels / 28,835 tons. On the same day, the TNN survey company, together with the terminal representative and the chief officer of the "Xique," jointly prepared a vessel ullage report after the crude oil was loaded, which recorded the actual loaded quantity as 210,286.282 barrels / 28,680.549 tons net at 60°F, 154.451 tons less than recorded in the bill of lading. The vessel "Xique" arrived at the port of destination, Zhoushan, on May 15 of the same year. During discharge, the consignee commissioned CCIQ to survey the quantity of crude oil discharged from the vessel into the C-05 shore tank at Aoshan Oil Depot. Meanwhile, the chief officer of the "Xique," together with CCIQ surveyors, prepared a vessel ullage report bearing the letterhead of the defendant Pan Cosmos, which stated the quantity of crude oil before discharge as 210,162 barrels / 28,693.417 tons net at 60°F, 141.583 tons less than recorded in the bill of lading, but 12.868 tons more than recorded in the loading port ullage report. From May 15 to 17 of the same year, the cargo was fully discharged, and the chief officer of the "Xique," together with CCIQ surveyors and the consignee's representative, jointly signed a dry tank report. On May 21 of the same year, CCIQ issued a weight certificate, stating: based on the liquid depth measured before and after the input into the C-05 shore tank at Aoshan Oil Depot, and after corresponding corrections for liquid temperature, density, and water according to the calibration table, the calculated weight of the input oil was 28,339.606 tons, or 206,506 barrels, 495.394 tons less than the weight recorded in the bill of lading. Subsequently, the price under the crude oil trade contract was reduced for certain reasons. The seller issued an invoice dated May 13, stating the quantity of crude oil as 211,200 barrels / 28,835 tons, the price as USD 25.580 per barrel CIF Zhoushan, China, and the total amount as USD 5,402,496. On June 5, 2002, China International Petrochemical Company paid the sum of USD 5,402,496 to Unipec Asia Company Ltd., which was USD 139,180.80 less than the contract price. On December 27, 2002, the plaintiff, based on the discrepancy between the CCIQ Weight Certificate and the bill of lading quantity, and after deducting the 5‰ natural loss rate at the unit price stipulated in the insurance policy, paid an indemnity of USD 67,497.62 to the insured, China International Petrochemical Company. On January 6, 2003, the insured issued a letter of subrogation to the plaintiff. On March 7 of the same year, the UK P&I Club issued a letter of guarantee to the plaintiff, confirming that the owner of the vessel "Xique" was the defendant Copper River, that the vessel was not under a bareboat charter for the voyage in question, and that the vessel was actually managed and operated by Pan Cosmos.

The issues in dispute in this case were: 1. Whether the carrier was obliged to deliver the crude oil in the quantity recorded in the bill of lading; 2. Whether a shortage of cargo occurred during the carrier's period of responsibility in this case.

The Ningbo Maritime Court held that:

1. Regarding the issue of whether the carrier was obliged to deliver the crude oil in the quantity recorded in the bill of lading

Article 252(1) of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Maritime Code) provides: "If the loss of or damage to the subject matter insured within the scope of cover is caused by a third party, the right of the insured to demand compensation from the third party shall be subrogated to the insurer from the date the insurer pays the indemnity." The plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch, has actually paid the insurance indemnity to the insured, China International Petrochemical Company, under the cargo insurance contract and has lawfully obtained the right to claim compensation from the carrier.

Article 75 of the Maritime Code provides: "If the carrier or the person issuing the bill of lading on his behalf knows or has reasonable grounds to suspect that the particulars of the goods, such as their description, marks, number of packages or pieces, weight or volume, as recorded in the bill of lading do not correspond to the goods actually received, or, where a shipped bill of lading is issued, to the goods loaded on board, or if he has had no reasonable means of checking the particulars, he may insert a reservation in the bill of lading specifying the inaccuracies, the grounds for suspicion or the lack of reasonable means of checking." Article 76 provides: "If the carrier or the person issuing the bill of lading on his behalf fails to make a reservation in the bill of lading regarding the apparent condition of the goods, the goods shall be deemed to be in apparent good condition." Article 77 provides: "Except for the reservations made in accordance with Article 75 of this Code, a bill of lading issued by the carrier or the person issuing the bill of lading on his behalf shall be prima facie evidence that the carrier has received the goods as described therein or that the goods have been loaded on board; such evidence shall not be rebutted by evidence to the contrary adduced by the carrier against a third party, including a consignee, who has taken the bill of lading in good faith." According to the above provisions, the particulars of the goods in the bill of lading are provided by the shipper. When the carrier knows or has reasonable grounds to suspect that the goods received or loaded on board do not correspond to the description in the bill of lading, or if there is no reasonable means of checking, the carrier may insert a reservation in the bill of lading. Once a reservation is made, it negates the effect of the bill of lading to a certain extent, and the carrier may be exempted from liability within the scope and items of the reservation. A clean bill of lading without reservations is sufficient to indicate that the carrier fully acknowledges the description of the goods in the bill of lading, and the carrier shall deliver the goods as described therein. A bill of lading is a document of title. A person who takes the bill of lading in good faith is entitled to rely on the expectation that the goods to be received are those described in the bill of lading. Evidence adduced by the carrier against a third party, including a consignee, who has taken the bill of lading in good faith, showing that the goods actually received or loaded on board differ from the description in the clean bill of lading, is insufficient to rebut the description in the bill of lading. If the goods delivered by the carrier do not correspond to the description in the bill of lading, the carrier shall bear corresponding liability. Accordingly, even if the carrier in this case submitted the loading port ullage report to prove that the goods actually received or loaded on board differed from the description in the bill of lading, the consignee is still entitled to take delivery of the goods from the carrier in accordance with the bill of lading. The defendants, Copper River and Pan Cosmos, have no legal basis for their contention that the loading port ullage report is binding on the consignee. The carrier must deliver the goods in the quantity recorded in the bill of lading.

2. Regarding the issue of whether a shortage of cargo occurred during the carrier's period of responsibility in this case

In the crude oil trade and transport industry, three methods of measurement are commonly used for the delivery and receipt of crude oil quantities: flow meter measurement, tank measurement, and vessel measurement. However, there is no uniform industry requirement. Sometimes different measurement methods are used at the loading and discharging ports, which makes it difficult to confirm the quantity of crude oil delivered. In this case, the crude oil trade contract only required the seller to provide the bill of lading, certificate of quantity, loading port ullage report, invoice, and other documents for the cargo in question, while the relevant transport documents also did not stipulate the method of measurement for delivery at the discharging port. Three different methods of measurement were actually used for the delivery of the cargo in this case: flow meter measurement, vessel ullage measurement, and shore tank measurement. Specifically, the shipper and the survey company at the loading port used flow meter measurement data to confirm the net weight, and the carrier issued the bill of lading based on that; the surveyors at the loading port, together with the terminal representative and the chief officer of the "Xique," jointly prepared a vessel ullage report to confirm the net weight; before discharge at the port of destination, the consignee commissioned CCIQ to survey the weight of the cargo discharged into the shore tank before and after the transfer, and the carrier also prepared an ullage report together with CCIQ. Three different methods of measurement for cargo delivery will inevitably produce three different survey results. An analysis of the ullage reports at the loading and discharging ports shows that the quantity recorded in the loading port ullage report was 210,286.282 barrels / 28,680.549 tons net at 60°F, and the quantity recorded in the discharging port ullage report was 210,162 barrels / 28,693.417 tons net at 60°F. Both ullage reports were signed and confirmed by surveyors, indicating that the cargo quantities confirmed at the two ports were essentially equal, and that there was no fault in the carrier's care of the cargo during the voyage. Furthermore, the dry tank report, signed by three parties, recorded that after the discharge operation was completed, there was no residual crude oil in any of the cargo tanks of the "Xique," and that all tanks had been emptied. This further proves that the carrier has fulfilled its delivery obligation. The differences between the quantity in the discharging port ullage report and the quantity in the bill of lading are all within the 0.5% tolerance for cargo discrepancy permitted by international practice in the maritime oil trade. However, the quantity recorded in the CCIQ Weight Certificate was calculated based on the depth data measured before and after the cargo was discharged into the shore tank, i.e., CCIQ did not use the same flow meter measurement method as at the loading port. After a comparative analysis of the discharging port ullage report, the dry tank report, and the CCIQ Weight Certificate, it is concluded that, in this case, the discharging port ullage report and the dry tank report have stronger probative value and evidentiary advantage over the CCIQ Weight Certificate in proving the quantity of cargo delivered by the carrier. The fact that the cargo shortage exceeds 0.5% cannot be established. Therefore, the plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch, relying on the difference in cargo quantity between the bill of lading and the CCIQ Weight Certificate, claims that a shortage occurred. This claim is unfounded, and its lawsuit lacks factual basis.

In conclusion, the Ningbo Maritime Court, on July 27, 2004, rendered the following judgment:

The claims of the plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch, are dismissed.

The court acceptance fee of RMB 21,208 and the investigation and evidence collection fee of RMB 2,000 shall be borne by the plaintiff, PICC Beijing Branch.

PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited, Beijing Branch (hereinafter "PICC Beijing Branch") refused to accept the first-instance judgment and appealed to the Zhejiang High People's Court, arguing as follows: 1. The first-instance court erred in finding that the Appellant's claim of a cargo shortage based on the difference in cargo quantity between the bill of lading and the CCIQ weight certificate was unfounded. 2. The first-instance court erred in finding that whether a cargo shortage existed should be determined by comparing the cargo quantity stated on the bill of lading with the cargo quantity recorded in the ullage report and dry tank report at the discharge port. 3. Technically, the accuracy of tank measurement is far lower than that of shore tank measurement. The first-instance court failed to consider the factor of cargo clingage and the VEF (Vessel Experience Factor). Therefore, the first-instance court erred in finding that the ullage report and dry tank report at the discharge port had stronger probative force and evidentiary advantage over the CCIQ weight certificate in proving the cargo quantity. It requested the court of second instance to set aside the original judgment and render a new judgment in accordance with the law.

Appellant PICC Beijing Branch did not submit new evidence.

Appellees Tonghe Company and Huanyu Company responded in writing as follows: 1. The first-instance court's finding that the carrier should deliver the cargo according to the quantity stated on the bill of lading was based on the function of the bill of lading. A finding of authenticity of the CCIQ weight certificate does not mean that this certificate can be used as the basis for determining the occurrence of a shortage. Because the CCIQ weight certificate was not comparable, the first-instance court was correct in finding that the Appellant's claim of a cargo shortage based on the difference in cargo quantity between the bill of lading and the CCIQ weight certificate was unfounded. 2. Where multiple measurement methods exist, if the parties have not agreed in advance, the same measurement method should be used to determine whether a shortage has occurred. CCIQ had already confirmed the ullage report and dry tank report for the discharge port. Therefore, to determine whether a cargo shortage occurred in this case, the cargo quantity recorded on the bill of lading should be compared with the cargo quantity recorded in the ullage report and dry tank report at the discharge port. The first-instance judgment was fair and reasonable. 3. The Appellant's claim that the accuracy of tank measurement is far lower than that of shore tank measurement has no scientific basis, and its claim of cargo clingage also has no basis. Therefore, the first-instance court was correct in finding that the ullage report and dry tank report at the discharge port had stronger probative force and evidentiary advantage over the CCIQ weight certificate in confirming the cargo quantity. It requested that the appeal be dismissed.

Appellees Tonghe Company and Huanyu Company did not provide new evidence.

Upon the second-instance trial, the Zhejiang High People's Court confirmed the facts found by the first-instance court.

The Zhejiang High People's Court held in the second instance as follows:

In this case, where the crude oil sales contract and transport documents did not stipulate the method of cargo measurement for delivery at the loading and discharge ports, and where three different measurement methods—flow meter measurement, tank measurement, and tanker tank measurement—were actually adopted, the determination of which method was more accurate should be analyzed based on the specific facts of the case. Article 46, paragraph 1 of the Maritime Code provides: "The carrier's responsibility for the goods carried in containers covers the entire period from the time the goods are taken over by the carrier at the port of loading to the time the goods are delivered at the port of discharge, during which the goods are under the charge of the carrier. The carrier's responsibility for the goods not carried in containers covers the entire period from the time the goods are loaded on board the ship to the time the goods are discharged from the ship, during which the goods are under the charge of the carrier. During the period of the carrier's responsibility, the carrier shall be liable for the loss of or damage to the goods, except as otherwise provided in this Section." Therefore, the carrier's period of responsibility for goods not carried in containers is the entire period during which the goods are under the charge of the carrier. In this case, during the period from when the cargo was discharged from the ship to when it was transported through the pipeline to the shore tank, the cargo was not entirely under the charge of the carrier. Consequently, it was not entirely reasonable to take the quantity of the cargo after it entered the shore tank as the discharge quantity in this case and to bind the carrier accordingly. As to whether there were factors such as "clinging" affecting the accuracy of tanker tank measurement, as claimed by Appellant PICC Beijing Branch, the Appellant did not provide sufficient evidence, nor did it prove that the carrier had failed to follow the consignee's instructions or industry practices in measurement. Furthermore, the ullage reports at both the loading and discharge ports clearly recorded the cargo quantity, and the recorded cargo quantities were very close. Therefore, the two ullage reports and the dry tank report confirmed by CCIQ can serve as the basis for determining the cargo quantity in this case.

Where different measurement methods exist, leading to discrepancies, the determination of whether a cargo shortage exists should be made through a comprehensive assessment based on the facts of the case and the probative force of the various pieces of evidence. Since tanker tank measurement was used for the cargo in question at the loading port, and the same measurement method was adopted at the discharge port, tanker tank measurement can be used as the measurement method for settling the case. At the same time, to be consistent with the carrier's period of responsibility, the cargo quantity recorded on the bill of lading should be compared with the discharge quantity recorded in the ullage report and dry tank report at the discharge port, in order to determine whether a cargo shortage occurred. Given that the difference in cargo quantity between the two was 141.583 tons, which falls within the reasonable shortage rate of 0.5% generally permitted by international crude oil trade practices, the Appellant PICC Beijing Branch's claim of a cargo shortage had no factual basis, and the carrier should not be held liable for damages according to law.

In summary, the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. The appeal by Appellant PICC Beijing Branch lacked factual and legal basis, and its appeal request was not supported.

Accordingly, in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Zhejiang High People's Court rendered the following judgment on November 29, 2004:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 21,208 shall be borne by Appellant PICC Beijing Branch.

This judgment is final.
